115	**[5. Alternative Treatments]{.underline}**
116	
117	Participants should be aware that participation in this study is not the only option for managing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Enrollment in this clinical trial is entirely voluntary, and participants who choose not to enroll or who withdraw from the study at any time will continue to have access to standard-of-care treatments for T2DM through their personal physicians. The following standard-of-care treatments are available and may be discussed with the participant\'s personal physician:
118	
119	**(1) Metformin.** Metformin is the established first-line oral pharmacotherapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. It has well-documented efficacy in reducing HbA1c levels and is generally well-tolerated. Common side effects include gastrointestinal disturbance (nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort), which typically resolve over time. Metformin is widely available, is available in generic form, and has decades of clinical experience supporting its safety profile in the treatment of T2DM.
120	
121	**(2) Insulin Therapy.** Insulin therapy remains a cornerstone of diabetes management, particularly for patients who do not achieve adequate glycemic control with oral agents alone. Available insulin regimens include basal insulin (long-acting formulations administered once daily), prandial insulin (rapid-acting formulations administered before meals), and premixed insulin preparations. Insulin therapy is indicated across the continuum of T2DM management and requires regular self-monitoring of blood glucose.
122	
123	**(3) SGLT-2 Inhibitors.** Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors represent a class of oral medications that lower blood glucose by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney, thereby promoting urinary glucose excretion. In addition to glycemic benefits, multiple large-scale clinical trials have demonstrated cardiovascular and renal protective effects with SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy.
124	
125	In addition to the above, other approved pharmacologic therapies for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus---including sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors, and other GLP-1 receptor agonists---may also be appropriate depending on individual patient circumstances, comorbidities, treatment goals, and risk factors. Participants should consult with their treating physician to determine the most suitable treatment approach for their individual situation.
126	
127	Participation in this study is voluntary. Participants may choose any available standard-of-care treatment for T2DM instead of or in addition to participation in this study. Per 21 CFR 50.25(a)(4), information regarding appropriate alternative procedures or courses of treatment, if any, that might be advantageous to the subject, must be included in the informed consent form provided to all potential participants.

129	**[6. Investigational Product]{.underline}**
130	
131	**6.1 Description.** The investigational product is PNC-4187 (tiravamide --- working name; not yet an approved generic name). PNC-4187 is a GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonist formulated for subcutaneous injection. The drug is supplied in a pre-filled, single-use injection pen designed for once-weekly administration. The route of administration is subcutaneous injection into the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm, with rotation of injection sites recommended.

133	The comparator is a matching placebo, supplied in an identical pre-filled pen that does not contain the active pharmaceutical ingredient. 136	
137	PNC-4187 is administered according to the following mandatory dose escalation schedule to mitigate gastrointestinal tolerability concerns:

140	>
141	> • **Weeks 5--8:** 1.0 mg PNC-4187 (or matching placebo) administered subcutaneously once weekly.
142	>
143	> • **Weeks 9--52:** 2.0 mg PNC-4187 (or matching placebo) administered subcutaneously once weekly.

Dose reduction decisions must be documented in the participant\'s source records and reported on the case report form. Participants who cannot tolerate the minimum dose of 0.5 mg should be evaluated for study discontinuation.

285	**9.2 Black Box Warning --- Thyroid C-Cell Tumors**
286	
287	The following Black Box Warning is based on preclinical findings from animal carcinogenicity studies with PNC-4187 and must be prominently disclosed to all potential study participants:
288	
289	**WARNING: RISK OF THYROID C-CELL TUMORS**
290	
291	**In animal studies, PNC-4187 caused thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in rats and mice. It is unknown whether PNC-4187 causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including MTC, in humans.**
292	
293	**PNC-4187 is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC or in patients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).**
294	
295	In 2-year carcinogenicity studies conducted with PNC-4187, a statistically significant increase in the incidence of thyroid C-cell tumors (both adenomas and carcinomas) was observed in both male and female rats at all doses tested (at and above 0.5 mg/kg/week). In mice, a statistically significant increase in thyroid C-cell tumors was observed at doses at and above 2.0 mg/kg/week. The lowest dose at which thyroid C-cell tumors were observed in rats corresponds to approximately 0.3 times the maximum recommended human dose on a mg/m² basis. The clinical relevance of these preclinical findings to humans has not been established, as the GLP-1 receptor-mediated mechanism of thyroid C-cell tumor development in rodents may not directly translate to human physiology due to differences in GLP-1 receptor expression on human thyroid C-cells.
296	
297	As a precautionary measure, serum calcitonin monitoring is performed at the Screening visit (Visit 1), Week 24 (Visit 9), and Week 52 (Visit 16). Participants with markedly elevated calcitonin levels or signs or symptoms suggestive of thyroid malignancy will be referred for further evaluation and may be discontinued from the study.
298	
299	Participants with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2) are excluded from participation in this study (see Section 4.2, Exclusion Criteria). This warning must be prominently disclosed in the informed consent form provided to all potential study participants, per 21 CFR 50.25(a)(2), which requires disclosure of any reasonably foreseeable risks or discomforts to the subject.

399	**[13. Statistical Considerations]{.underline}**
400	
401	The study is designed with a target enrollment of 500 participants randomized in a 2:1 ratio, yielding approximately 333 participants in the PNC-4187 treatment group and 167 participants in the placebo group. This sample size provides greater than 90% statistical power to detect a clinically meaningful difference of 0.5% in the change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 52 between PNC-4187 and placebo, under the following assumptions: a common standard deviation of 1.2% for HbA1c change from baseline, a two-sided significance level (alpha) of 0.05, and an anticipated dropout rate of approximately 15% over the 52-week treatment period. The sample size calculation accounts for the dropout rate by inflating the required number of evaluable participants to ensure adequate power in the per-protocol and modified intent-to-treat analysis populations.
402	
403	The primary efficacy analysis will employ a mixed-model repeated measures (MMRM) approach to analyze the change from baseline in HbA1c at Week 52. The MMRM model will include treatment group, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, baseline HbA1c value, and the stratification factors (baseline HbA1c category and background metformin use) as covariates. An unstructured covariance matrix will be used to model within-subject correlations. The primary comparison will be the least-squares mean difference between PNC-4187 and placebo at Week 52, with a two-sided 95% confidence interval and corresponding p-value.
404	
405	Key secondary endpoints will be analyzed in the pre-specified hierarchical order described in Section 8.2 to control the family-wise Type I error rate at 0.05. Only if the primary endpoint achieves statistical significance will the first secondary endpoint be formally tested, and so forth through the testing hierarchy.
406	
407	The statistical analysis plan (SAP) has been developed and is maintained by Brenton Analytics Group. The SAP provides full details of all planned analyses, including handling of missing data, sensitivity analyses, subgroup analyses, and the definitions of the analysis populations (intent-to-treat, modified intent-to-treat, per-protocol, and safety populations).
408	
409	The pre-planned interim analysis was conducted at approximately 60% of target enrollment by the independent DSMB and was completed on November 15, 2024. The DSMB reviewed unblinded safety and efficacy data and recommended continuation of the study without modification. The interim analysis employed an O\'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending function to preserve the overall Type I error rate for the final analysis.

*Protocol PNC-4187-301 (IND 158432; NCT05234817) \| Informed Consent Form Version 3.0 (March 15, 2025)*

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Privileged and Confidential**     Attorney Work Product / Prepared in Anticipation of FDA Inspection
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **To**                              Sarah Lindquist, Partner, Hartwell & Calloway LLP

  **Cc**                              David Okonkwo, Associate

  **Re**                              Pinnacle Health Systems: PNC-4187-301 ICF v3.0 review against Protocol Synopsis, CIRB Continuing Review #2 approval letter (Feb. 7, 2025) and site FDA inspection-readiness checklist (reviewed June 8-10, 2025)

  **Inspection date**                 August 18, 2025 (per Site Documentation checklist, Item 11)
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Executive Summary

Bottom line: ICF Version 3.0 is not inspection-ready. It is missing or materially defective on at least five required elements of informed consent (21 CFR 50.25(a)(2), (a)(4), (a)(6), (a)(7) and (a)(8), plus 50.25(c)), it conflicts with the protocol on compensation, visit count and data recipients, and it still carries the superseded CIRB telephone number the CIRB has now twice ordered corrected. The site's internal FDA checklist marks every one of these items "Complete" and should not be shown to an investigator in its current form.

**Highest-risk findings (detail in Parts III-V):**

1.  No disclosure of alternative treatments (50.25(a)(4)). The ICF has no alternatives section at all; the protocol (Section 5) lists metformin, insulin, SGLT-2 inhibitors and other agents and expressly states that 50.25(a)(4) requires this content in the ICF. Checklist Item 4 marks this "Complete" citing ICF Section 7, which is the confidentiality section.

2.  Boxed Warning for thyroid C-cell tumors omitted (50.25(a)(2)). The protocol (Section 9.2) and Investigator's Brochure Ed. 4 require prominent disclosure that PNC-4187 caused thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in rats and mice, and that it is contraindicated with personal/family history of MTC or MEN 2. The ICF says only "Thyroid problems (rare)" and lists it among side effects in earlier studies.

3.  CIRB contact number wrong (50.25(a)(7); CIRB Stipulation 2). The ICF lists (704) 555-3829; the CIRB letterhead, Stipulation 2 and the protocol give (704) 555-3920. This is the second consecutive continuing review to raise the issue, and the checklist (Items 7 and 21) records the wrong number as "verified."

4.  Voluntariness statement incomplete (50.25(a)(8)). The ICF never states that refusal to participate involves no penalty or loss of benefits to which the subject is otherwise entitled, or that the subject may discontinue without penalty or loss of benefits. The protocol (Section 12.1) contains the required language; the ICF does not.

5.  Injury compensation language incomplete and inconsistent (50.25(a)(6)). The ICF says Pinnacle "will provide medical treatment" but does not say who pays. The protocol (Section 10.3) commits Pinnacle to bear the cost, with no billing of the participant or insurer, for injuries "directly" attributable to the study drug or procedures, as determined by the PI with the sponsor. The ICF is both less informative and arguably broader than the protocol.

6.  Compensation understated: the ICF gives \$50 per visit, about 16 visits, \$800 maximum, paid per visit by check or gift card. The protocol (Section 10.1), whose amount the CIRB reviewed for undue influence, gives \$75 per visit, 18 visits, \$1,350 maximum, paid quarterly by check or electronic payment. Participants who sign the ICF are being told they will get \$550 less than the protocol provides.

7.  Undisclosed data recipients and commercial partner. The ICF refers only to an unnamed "research partner." The protocol (Section 11) identifies Ridgeline Pharmaceuticals (co-development partner, drug manufacturer, funder) as receiving coded data for regulatory submissions and product development, plus Brenton Analytics Group (CRO) and Crescent Laboratories (central lab, specimen storage). Ridgeline monitors may also inspect records (Protocol Section 15). The PI holds roughly \$87,500 of Ridgeline equity (Form FDA 3455).

8.  CIRB Stipulation 4 (re-consent) missed. All enrolled participants had to be re-consented on v3.0 by May 20, 2025. As of the June checklist, only 298 of 412 were done, 114 were outstanding, and the site has set its own target of July 31, 2025. This is noncompliance with an IRB condition of approval and must be reported to the CIRB. Stipulation 1 (revised ICF due March 9, 2025) was also met late: v3.0 is dated March 15 and was approved March 21, 2025.

9.  No ClinicalTrials.gov statement (50.25(c)). The study is an IND-phase applicable clinical trial (NCT05234817). The mandatory verbatim statement is absent, and the checklist does not test for it.

10. No HIPAA authorization meeting 45 CFR 164.508(c). The site relies on ICF Section 7 as its authorization (Regulatory Files Item 18), but Section 7 has none of the required core elements: a specific description of the PHI, named recipients, an expiration, the right to revoke, a redisclosure notice, and a signature on the authorization itself.

Recommended path: (1) prepare ICF v4.0 correcting every item in Part II and submit it to the CIRB now, with a cover letter that self-reports the late Stipulation 1 submission, the overdue Stipulation 4 re-consent and the repeated contact-number error; (2) correct and re-perform the inspection checklist through a reviewer independent of the study team; (3) open a CAPA covering consent-form version control and QC. Before the August 18, 2025 inspection, prepare a short, accurate narrative for the investigator on each of these points. Do not rely on the current checklist.

*Severity scale: Critical = missing required consent element, or IRB-condition noncompliance likely to draw a Form FDA 483 observation and requiring subject notification; High = material inaccuracy or incomplete element; Medium = inconsistency requiring correction in the next ICF version; Low = housekeeping or advisory.*

I wrote the ICF review report and validated it: the validation script passed, and parse-doc reads it back in full. It concludes that ICF v3.0 is not ready for the August 18, 2025 FDA inspection: five basic elements of 21 CFR 50.25(a) fail ((a)(2), (a)(4), (a)(6), (a)(7), (a)(8)), and so does the 50.25(c) ClinicalTrials.gov statement, while the site's own checklist marks every item "Complete."

The report also extracts the key terms, rates each 50.25 element, and lists 22 discrepancies across the four documents. The main ones are: the thyroid tumor warning is missing, the IRB phone number is still the old one, pay is $50/16 visits/$800 against the protocol's $75/18/$1,350, and Ridgeline is not named. Re-consent to the IRB's May 20 deadline is not done (114 of 412). Other parts cover the checklist's errors, the status of each IRB condition, and a remediation plan.
